list.listitem: Suspect epiglottitis in any child or adult with abrupt onset of rapidly progressive sore throat, fever, dysphagia, and muffled voice. C
Diagnosis depends on clinical suspicion, confirmed by direct visualization of the epiglottis. C

Airway management and administration of parenteral antibiotics (eg, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, cefuroxime, ampicillin/sulbactam) are priorities for treatment. A In cases of impending airway obstruction, an immediate definitive airway, either an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy, is needed; this procedure is ideally performed in the operating room. C
Adults with patent airways and no dyspnea may be managed with close observation in an ICU setting rather than immediate intubation. B

background.definition: Epiglottitis is a rare but potentially life-threatening infectious inflammation of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic structures; it occurs in both children and adults.

list.listitem: Estimates of annual incidence rates range from 0.97 to 2.8 cases per 100,000 for adults and 0.5 per 100,000 population for children.

Incidence rates among children are likely decreasing; in a study in Sweden, the incidence rate was 0.98 cases/100,000/year compared with 4.5 cases/100,000/year before instituting a childhood Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) vaccination program.
There is a slight male predominance, with no seasonal variation.
Age in children has shifted to older children, with the mean age rising from 5.8 years between 1990 and 1997 to 11.6 years between 1998 and 2002.

In an adult population study in Finland (1989-2009), the incidence of supraglottis was found to be increasing from 1.88 (first decade) to 4.73 per 100,000 cases. Isolated inflammation of the epiglottis was found in 51/308 cases (17%) and streptococcus was the most common organism in throat cultures.

In a case series using a national database, 342 patients were admitted for epiglottitis with airway intervention; 40 of whom were under the age of 19 years. Of the children, mean age was 4.3 years (SD = 6.0 years), average length of stay was 15.6 days (SD = 33.9) and average total charges were $74,931 (SD = $163,387, range = $3342-$938,512).
Causes are infectious and non-infectious. There is no predominant etiologic pathogen. Before widespread Hib vaccination, Hib was the predominant pathogen in both children and adults.
Since the widespread use of the vaccine, Hib epiglottitis is much less common in children, but may still occur, even in fully immunized children. Rates in adults have remained constant.

Other pathogens in adults and children include H. influenza type A (Hia), type F, and nontypeable strains; Streptococcus pneumoniae; Staphylococcus aureus; beta-hemolytic streptococci; viruses including herpes simplex, and fungi (eg, Aspergillus spp and Candida albicans). In Native Alaskan children, Hia has become a major invasive bacterial disease with an incidence rate of 204/100,000.
Traumatic epiglottitis can occur from direct trauma, thermal injury, or ingestion of corrosives.
Hyperplastic epiglottis caused by chronic inflammation has been reported.
Infectious organisms are often from the nasopharynx.
Local cellulitis and inflammation occur in the epiglottis, the aryepiglottic folds, and other adjacent supraglottic tissue.
The swollen epiglottis causes airway compromise or obstruction.
Any child or adult with abrupt onset of rapidly progressive sore throat, fever, dysphagia, and muffled voice should be suspected of having epiglottitis. C
Definitive diagnosis with visualization of the epiglottis should not be delayed. C
Lateral neck radiographs should be considered only in a patient with subacute illness, when other diagnoses are being considered and definitive diagnosis is not delayed. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Barking cough, not uncomfortable lying down, normal-appearing epiglottis on examination, viral prodrome
Clinical features similar, normal-appearing epiglottis on examination, diagnosis by bronchoscopy
Usually not as toxic appearing or anxious, normal-appearing epiglottis on examination

Differential.Differential_Name: Foreign body in the larynx or vallecula

Differential.Differential_Features: History of exposure to offending agent, no fever, localized swelling

list.listitem: Children : classic presentation is abrupt onset, rapidly progressive, fever, severe sore throat, dysphagia, drooling, "hot potato" voice. Children often appear anxious, restless, or toxic and may assume a unique posture with arms back, trunk forward, neck hyperextended, and chin forward (tripod position). Stridor and respiratory difficulty are much more common than in adults, occurring in about 80% of cases versus 5% to 20% in adults.

In one study comparing 109 children with epiglottis to 102 children with croup, the most distinguishing features were the presence of drooling (sensitivity 0.79, 95% CI, 0.70-0.86 and specificity 0.94, 95% CI, 0.88-0.97) for epiglottitis and cough (sensitivity 1.00, 95% CI, 0.96-1.00 and specificity 0.98, 95% CI, 0.93-0.99) for croup. Other reliable identifying features for epiglottis were a preference to sit, refusal to swallow and dysphagia.

Adults : usually also abrupt onset and rapidly progressive fever, severe sore throat, odynophagia/dysphagia, and muffled voice. Adults may have preceding upper respiratory infection symptoms and may have tenderness over the anterior neck (the hyoid bone). Based on retrospective studies, the most common presenting symptoms in adults include sore throat (91%-100%) and odynophagia (82%-94%). The most common signs include anterior neck tenderness (79%), tachycardia (54%), and muffled voice (48%-79%).
Stridor is a late finding for both children and adults.

Predictors of severe epiglottitis among 6,072 Japanese adults with acute epiglottitis from 599 hospitals included older age, male sex (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 1.60; 95% CI, 1.28-2.00), body mass index >25.0 kg/m2 (OR 1.31; 95% CI, 1.05-1.63), diabetes mellitus (OR 1.41; 95% CI, 1.06-1.86), epiglottic cyst (OR 2.90; 95% CI, 1.46-5.78), pneumonia (OR 2.90; 95% CI, 1.73-4.86), and care in an academic hospital (OR 1.56; 95% CI, 1.21-2.00).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 30 studies including 10,148 adults with epiglottitis, found 3 factors that were associated with need for airway intervention - presence of an abscess, stridor, or a history of diabetes mellitus. Need for securing the airway occurred in 10.9% of cases.

Diagnosis should be considered based on clinical grounds. Although the diagnosis is confirmed by specialty consultation (usually ENT) for direct endoscopic visualization of the epiglottis, treatment should not be delayed while awaiting definitive diagnosis.

Delay in definitive diagnosis and treatment may be life threatening. Therefore, although lateral neck radiographs have been a mainstay of diagnosis in the past, they are rarely necessary, except in subacute cases and when other diagnoses are strongly considered. Published studies report sensitivity of lateral radiographs of 38% to 96%.

In case-control study including 260 patients with epiglottitis and 1166 controls with normal lateral neck radiographs, the highest predictive values for epiglottitis were epiglottis base cutoff value 5.02 mm (area under the curve [AUC] 0.99), epiglottis tip cutoff value 4.84 (AUC 0.97), and aryepiglottic fold cutoff value 6.59 mm (AUC 0.88).

Bedside sonography can be useful. Authors of a small study found anteroposterior diameter of the epiglottis was significantly higher for patients with epiglottitis compared to healthy control subjects; there was no overlap in values for both lateral edges—3.7 and 3.6 mm for right and left edges vs. 3.2 mm for controls.
Most children and adults have an elevated leukocyte count. Microbial diagnosis is made by culture of the organism from blood or the surface of the epiglottis.

Suspect epiglottitis in patients presenting with abrupt onset of fever, severe sore throat, dysphagia, drooling, muffled or "hot potato" voice, and tenderness over hyoid bone. Tripod position may be seen, with arms back, trunk forward, neck hyperextended, and chin forward.
All patients with suspected epiglottitis should have immediate consultation for confirmation of the diagnosis by direct visualization (see ).
Immediately consult anesthesiology, ENT, or surgery for direct visualization when epiglottitis is suspected. Airway maintenance, with intubation if needed, is the first priority. C
Adults with patent airways and no dyspnea may be managed with close observation in the ICU instead of immediate intubation. B

Empiric parenteral antibiotics with efficacy against S. aureus, pneumococcus, group A streptococcus, and H. influenza (eg, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, cefuroxime, ampicillin/sulbactam) should be started immediately after airway management. A
Steroids have commonly been used, but there are no good clinical trials to evaluate the efficacy. C

Use empiric antibiotic therapy with coverage against S. aureus, pneumococci, group A streptococcus, and H. influenzae. Data from RCTs are limited but generally support ceftriaxone and related cephalosporins.

Suggested regimens are ceftriaxone (pediatric: 75-100 mg/kg/d IV every 12-24 hours, adult: 1-2 g IV every 12-24 hours), cefotaxime (pediatric: 150-200 mg/kg/d IV divided four times daily, adult: 2 g IV every 4-8 hours), cefuroxime (pediatric: 100-150 mg/kg/d IV divided three times daily, adult: 750 mg-1.5 g IV every 8 hours), ampicillin-sulbactam (pediatric: 300-600 mg/kg/d IV ampicillin divided every 6 hours, adult: 1.5-3 g IV every 6-8 hours, max 8 g/d ampicillin), or cefepime (pediatric: 100 mg/kg/d IV in two divided doses, adult: 2 g IV every 12 hours).

When there is concern for methicillin-resistant S. aureus, add clindamycin (pediatric: 30-40 mg/kg/d IV divided every 6-8 hours, adult: 600-1200 mg/d IV divided 2 to 4 times daily) or vancomycin (pediatric: 40-60 mg/kg/d IV divided 3 to 4 times daily, adult: 500-1000 mg IV every 12 hours, adjusted as needed).

In a case series from 2001 to 2015 in Denmark of 103 patients admitted with acute epiglottitis, there were no significant differences in clinical presentation, duration of hospitalization, admission to the ICU, or required change in antibiotic for the 83 patients initially treated with intravenous ampicillin compared with 20 patients given other antibiotics (4 for immune compromise, 1 for esophageal perforation 7 because of allergy and 8 for unspecified reasons. Six patients suffered complications and one patient died.
Therapy duration depends on patient response and is usually 7 to 10 days, although some older studies in the pre-Hib vaccine era found that shorter regimens were also effective.
Common practice is to give methylprednisolone, but no randomized trials have evaluated usefulness.
Household and daycare contacts should receive rifampin prophylaxis.
May require tracheostomy if edema prevents intubation to secure airway.
Allow children to assume comfortable position; do nothing to cause agitation.
In children, establish an artificial airway as soon as possible.
Nasotracheal intubation is preferable with tube diameter 0.5 to 1.0 mm smaller than would otherwise be used for that patient, tracheostomy only if unable to intubate because of severe edema.

Adults with any degree of dyspnea or greater than 50% obstruction of the upper airway should also be immediately intubated. Adults with a patent airway and no dyspnea may be closely monitored in an ICU.
If hypoxic, administer oxygen.
Immediate consultation with anesthesiology, ENT, and possibly surgery should be undertaken for any child or adult with suspected epiglottitis based on clinical presentation.
Epiglottic abscess is a potential complication and can be diagnosed on CT and managed with abscess drainage under local anesthesia.

Historically, there has been a high case fatality rate, with estimates ranging up to 50%. However, with the decreasing incidence of epiglottitis in children and increased awareness in adults, a more recent retrospective review found mortality rates of about 2% in children and 3% in adults. B

Based on data from 33,549 cases of adult epiglottitis from the National Emergency Department Sample from 2007 to 2014, average mortality was 1.01% or 42 deaths per year. The average patient age increased significantly from 47 to 51 years. A total of 11.8% of patients were coded as having obstruction and most (68.3%) were admitted to the hospital. Less than 1% received laryngoscopic or airway procedures in the ED and use of imaging was <10%.
In the large Japanese database study noted above, 9.4% developed severe epiglottitis and the 2-day mortality was 0.4%.

In a follow-up study of 34 adult patients admitted to the ICU with epiglottitis, thirteen (38%) required respiratory assistance, 9 (26%) required surgery, two died following hypoxemic cardiac arrest and five patients (15%) had sequelae at 1 year.
